Switch 2 Black Friday deals are officially HERE! It's the biggest day of the year for Nintendo savings, and the deals are zipping on in. My job is literally tracking deals — and I've been putting my Switch 2 through its paces for two years now. I'm here to track the best deals as they arrive. When I say we're live , we're live : I'm tracking deals by the minute.
Today, I recommend picking up the Nintendo Switch 2 Mario Kart World bundle for $50 off while you can. It's simply the best way to save and get a console for the holiday season, and it's way cheaper than both the Xbox and PS5. I gotta shout out Sonic X Shadow Generations on sale for $15 , some of the most fun I've had on my Switch 2 and the best Sonic game in decades. Not that that's a particularly high bar.
Don't go anywhere, as my colleagues and I will be here for the rest of Black Friday, bringing you the Nintendo Switch deals you can't miss.
Nintendo's Black Friday sale has arrived! For $499, you can pick up a Nintendo Switch 2 bundle that includes the console, Mario Kart World and a three-month Nintendo Switch Online membership. That's an $87 saving compared to purchasing each item individually. The deal also brings the bundle back to its original launch price, before the Switch 2's price increase. While it's not a brand-new discount, it's still a pretty compelling offer, particularly when you consider the rising prices of competing consoles like the PS5 and Xbox.
Don't miss the savings on this gaming headset. In our Turtle Beach Airlite Fit review , we loved this headset's ultra-comfortable design, its great sound quality, and its flip-to-mute mic. Better yet, we loved the affordable price, which has just got even better thanks to this deal.
The GameSir Super Nova is one of the cheapest controllers featuring Hall Effect triggers and thumbsticks, both of which lend you an edge in gaming. Compatible with a range of devices, the Super Nova boasts great gaming performance and it comes with a charging dock. It’s competitively priced and its companion software is user-friendly too. We rank it as the best Nintendo Switch 2 controller for shoppers on a budget.
The latest chapter in the Resident Evil series might just be the best yet, and that's really saying something. In Resident Evil Requiem , you play as both Leon S. Kennedy and newcomer Grace Ashcroft, and the whole game can be played in first- or third-person mode. It's chilling and exciting in equal measure, and an absolute must-play for action-horror fans.
Switch 2 owners can save and expand their console's storage with a 24% discount on this 512GB SanDisk microSD card.
Whether you want to play retro platformers or fighting games, there's no console with a game library as big as the Switch or Switch 2. If you want that arcade feel but with more modern controls, the 8BitDo All-Button Arcade Controller is just $48 on Amazon right now.
Leverless fightsticks without a joystick typically cost a whole lot more than this one. Likewise, you can customize it to your heart's content thanks to the hot-swappable switches underneath. While I haven't played with this one at home yet, I do have the original 8BitDo Arcade Stick for the Switch and I absolutely love it. While I don't play fighting games like our own Tony Polanco, I really like playing through Super Mario and other platformers using an arcade stick over a controller.
If you're looking to scratch that Wii Sports itch on your Switch 2, you're in luck as the recently released Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is just $44 at Amazon . Sure, this is just a $5 discount but for game that came out last month, that's not bad. Likewise, Switch Sports Resort is one of the cheaper Switch 2 games at $50.
In my Switch Sports Resort review , I said the game fixes my biggest gripe with Switch Sports as it now features a fully fleshed out single-player campaign. The free-roam traversal modes like flying a prop plane or riding a skateboard really help break up the action too.
Add more storage to your Switch 2 for less
With all of these great Switch 2 game discounts for Black Friday, you're probably going to fill up the console's 256GB internal drive fast. While the 1TB card is still quite expensive, you can pick up a SanDisk 512GB microSD Express Card for just $129 at Amazon right now. That's $70 off its normal price and quite a good deal considering how much storage has gone up recently.
"A quintessential outing in a galaxy far, far away" is how we described the game in our 4-star Star Wars Outlaws review . It delivers a true Star Wars experience, featuring four total worlds teeming with expansive maps and various side quests for hours of unending fun. Space-based combat and general gunplay are solid, too.
Right now, you can grab Star Wars Outlaws for just $15 at Amazon , and this deal saves you $44!
If you're looking for a long JRPG you can really sink your teeth into this winter, look no further than Persona 3: Reload. Right now, you can pick up Persona 3: Reload for just $25 on Amazon which is more than half off its normal price. Whether you enjoyed Persona 5 or just want a nice JRPG you can play for hours, Persona 3: Reload is a fantastic option. In my Persona 3: Reload review , I praised the game's quality of life improvements, new animations, vibrant visuals and fresh voice cast.
If you're a fan of the series that hasn't played the game responsible for the modern Persona formula yet, you owe it to yourself to give this one a shot, especially since you can now play in handheld mode.
Oh my goodness, Overcooked! All You Can Eat just dropped to its lowest ever price of just $9 at Nintendo ! This is an insane deal. Overcooked! and its sequel are mine and my partner's favorite couch co-op games, and this Black Friday deal (which includes both games and all DLCs) sweetens the game even more.
In this cartoon cooking simulator, you and up to three other players must chop, dice, prepare and serve dishes in quick succession — and don't forget to wash those dishes and put out the fires lest they burn your kitchen down. Each level lasts only a few minutes, and you can earn a tip multiplier if you deliver orders on time.
One of the best things about the Switch 2 being significantly more powerful than the original Switch is that it can now run some of the best games of the last and current console generation. Among these, Final Fantasy 7 Remake and Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth are some of the most impressive.
Sure, the open world of Rebirth won't look or run nearly as well as it does on other consoles or PC but with the Switch 2, you can explore the Gongaga Region on the go in handheld mode. If the Switch 2 is your main console, it's absolutely worth picking up both games in the FF7 Remake Trilogy before Final Fantasy VII Revelation comes out in April.
To be honest, now that the Nintendo Switch 2 Mario Kart World bundle is on sale for $499 , I recommend it as the best value bundle for most people. But if you're more into sports than racing or perhaps you just want your kids to move around a bit more, the Nintendo Switch 2 + Nintendo Switch Sports Resort bundle could be the one for you. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort provides plenty of variety with 12 sports and a large hub world to explore! Plus, all the games offer online and in-person multiplayer.

articles.title_orig: Canada’s Supreme Court largely upholds a Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.title_zh: Canada’s Supreme Court largely upholds a Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.content_orig:
Quebec's secularism law, Bill 21, has been almost completely upheld in a decision by the Supreme Court of Canada that affirms Quebec's legal authority to prevent some public-sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job.
"Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society," Chief Justice Richard Wagner said in the judgment.
The ruling means Quebec can impose the ban with one exception: it cannot apply to members of Quebec's National Assembly because doing so would infringe elected officials' democratic rights.
In their decision, the seven justices at the Supreme Court who heard the case addressed 10 issues that the 51 groups, individual appellants and interveners raised with the court, dismissing all appeals in the case.
Four of the Justices on the court, including Wagner, Suzanne Côté, Nicholas Kasirer and Malcolm Rowe ruled that Bill 21 is constitutionally valid while Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Sheilah Martin dissented, saying the law violates section 28 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to deliver a four to three ruling on constitutional validity.
When Bill 21 was adopted in 2019, it invoked clauses in both the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms that allow lawmakers to override some protected rights — but not democratic rights, such as the ability to vote or serve in elected office.
Once invoked, Section 33, the notwithstanding clause, prevents any judicial review of the legislation in question. After five years, the clause ceases to have any effect — unless it is re-enacted.
The Supreme Court was asked whether Section 33 of the federal Charter was improperly used to quash rights in Quebec in this case and ruled that Quebec's use of the clause was correct.
Justice Martin declined to address the issue of whether the notwithstanding clause was properly invoked, but the other six justices said it was used correctly for an effective seven to zero vote on that question.
Canada's top court upholds Quebec law banning some workers from wearing religious symbols
What's at stake as Canada's top court ruling on Quebec secularism law looms
Despite the controversy around using Section 33, the top court said it remains valid in this case because the Supreme Court "does not have the power to rewrite the Constitution of Canada or to enact amendments to it," the ruling said.
"It is not open to the courts to place additional limits on the exercise of the override power."
The Supreme Court also ruled that courts in Canada have the ability to issue a non-binding judicial declaration on rights that are overridden by use of the clause.
"Such declarations both vindicate affected individuals and promote democratic accountability by informing citizens how their representatives have chosen to temporarily override rights and freedoms," the ruling said.
While the judgment allows the Supreme Court to make such a declaration in this case, the seven justices on the court voted 4-3 against doing so at this time.
Carney responds after top court upholds most of Quebec's secularism law
Section 28 of the federal Charter states that all of the rights and freedoms enshrined by the Charter "are guaranteed equally to male and female persons."
During the four-day trial in March of this year, the Supreme Court heard arguments that Bill 21 violated Section 28, which is not one of the rights the notwithstanding clause can override.
Appellants said that Bill 21 violated that part of the Charter because most of the people who have lost their jobs as a result of the law have been Muslim women who wear hijabs, while Muslim men don't.
Bill 21 ruling is 'license for every government' to take away Canadians' rights: NCCM
In a 4-3 vote, the top court dismissed that claim, saying sex equality is a principle through which the Charter is interpreted, but that Section 28 does not establish "a standalone equality guarantee," separate from the broad equality rights already outlined in Section 15 of the Charter.
Justices Karakatsanis and O'Bonsawin disagreed, saying Section 28 does establish a substantive right in itself.
The notwithstanding clause "cannot shield legislation that infringes Section 28 by affecting Charter rights in a manner that undermines substantive equality between men and women," two of the dissenting justices said.
Justice Sheilah L. Martin also dissented from the majority on equality rights between the sexes, saying Bill 21 unequally restricts "a woman's right to respect her faith, freely express herself and to be free from discrimination based on religion and sex."
Another section of the federal Charter that the notwithstanding clause cannot override is Section 23 , which protects minority-language education rights, something the English Montreal School Board says Bill 21 violates, and on that basis should be thrown out.
"It is true that Bill 21 limits the ability of English-language school boards to hire, retain and promote certain persons as teachers, principals and vice principals of schools," justices Wagner, Suzanne Côté, Nicholas Kasirer and Malcolm Rowe said.
But, they added, the board had "not shown that this restriction interferes with a linguistic or cultural concern that is specific to the English-speaking minority."
Montreal's English school board chair 'disappointed' by Bill 21 ruling, says advocacy will continue
Martin declined to address that issue, saying that because she already decided Bill 21 should be thrown out because of how it violates equality between the sexes, the point is moot.
Karakatsanis and O’Bonsawi, however, said Bill 21 prevents teaching staff from "transmitting important elements of its culture, including multiculturalism and religious diversity."
They went on to say that these restrictions negatively impact "the legitimate linguistic and cultural concerns of the minority language rights holders and therefore should not apply to Quebec’s English-language school boards."
When Bill 21 was adopted, it specifically impacted educators like teachers and principals, police officers, government lawyers and even members of the province's legislature, including Quebec's minister of justice and the Speaker of the National Assembly by prohibiting them from wearing religious symbols while on the job.
The law also required these public-sector workers to do their jobs with their faces uncovered unless they need them covered for non-religious reasons such as a health issue or a disability.
Bill 21 is 'legislative racism' Premier Kinew says
In Friday's ruling all seven justices that heard the case agreed Bill 21 would prevent people from enjoying their democratic rights protected under Section three of the Charter, by preventing them from serving in Quebec's National Assembly.
Friday's ruling lined up with previous rulings from both the Quebec Superior Court and the Quebec Court of Appeal, which both ruled that Bill 21 should not apply to members of Quebec's legislature.
Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.

articles.title_orig: Mamdani targets Amazon on Black Friday as 150K customers push back against delivery crackdown
articles.title_zh: Mamdani targets Amazon on Black Friday as 150K customers push back against delivery crackdown
articles.content_orig:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani calls for passage of the Delivery Protection Act as Amazon warns the legislation could drive up consumer prices, disrupt deliveries and threaten thousands of local jobs. (Credit: @NYCMayor via X)
As Americans hunt for Black Friday bargains, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is pushing new regulations on Amazon that the retail giant warns could leave New Yorkers paying more for everything from groceries to Christmas gifts.
The Democratic Socialist mayor released a video Friday demanding passage of the Delivery Protection Act , union-backed legislation that would impose new licensing and employment requirements on delivery operations across the nation's largest city.
More than 150,000 Amazon customers have emailed their City Council members urging them to oppose the legislation since Nov. 19 , Amazon told Fox News Digital.
The figure is up from roughly 60,000 emails generated within the campaign's first 36 hours, as previously reported by FOX Business.
AMAZON WARNS NYC OF $5 FEES DUE TO MAYOR’S DELIVERY BILL; MAMDANI CRIES ‘GREED’
Mamdani doubled down on his planned bill in a Black Friday video as select New York City Amazon delivery workers lamented their working conditions. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images / Getty Images)
"It's Black Friday. The busiest — and most dangerous — time of year for delivery workers," Mamdani wrote on X. "Pass the Delivery Protection Act now."
The video features select delivery workers accusing Amazon of controlling their schedules, routes and uniforms while using subcontractors to shield itself from responsibility for working conditions.
Amazon has warned customers that the legislation could add up to $5 per order. An economic analysis cited by the company estimated annual consumer cost increases of between $409 and $664.
"If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it’s not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed," Mamdani wrote on X.
EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani exits after a news conference to announce that he has struck a deal with President Donald Trump to secure a 90-day delay on new rules for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), at City Hall on Novembe (Adam Gray/Getty Images / Getty Images)
The retail giant fired back in an email to Fox News Digital.
"It’s no secret that this legislation, as written, would threaten the livelihoods of more than 40 small delivery businesses we work with in New York City and the 5,000-plus New Yorkers they employ," Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel told Fox News Digital. "These are businesses embedded in communities across the five boroughs, delivering from facilities across New York City. It would also raise costs for New Yorkers."
The bill, sponsored by Democratic City Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, would require certain delivery facilities to obtain city licenses and directly employ workers performing core services. Amazon says the requirement would effectively prohibit its partnerships with independent delivery businesses.
According to Amazon's April testimony before the City Council, 25% of its local delivery partners are Black or Hispanic-owned and 10% are veteran-owned.
MAMDANI THANKS TRUMP FOR HELPING SMALL BUSINESSES IN NYC, NATIONWIDE: 'PRESIDENT HAS DELIVERED RELIEF'
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani holds a news conference to announce that he has struck a deal with President Donald Trump to secure a 90-day delay on new rules for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), at City Hall on November 13, (Adam Gray/Getty Images / Getty Images)
The legislation would also impose third-party training requirements and require employers to provide 30 days' notice before terminating workers, except in cases of egregious misconduct.
The International Brotherhood of Teamsters has championed the legislation as part of its fight for employment and collective bargaining rights for Amazon delivery workers. Mamdani joined Teamsters General President Sean O'Brien at an Oct. 22 rally demanding passage of the bill.
While private businesses would face new restrictions on subcontracting, the legislation explicitly excludes government entities, including New York City itself, from its definition of a covered facility operator.
Amazon told Fox News Digital that neither Mamdani nor Cabán has accepted its invitation to tour a local delivery facility and meet with the small-business owners and workers who could be affected.
"We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written. But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations and they haven’t taken us up on our offer to visit our sites and talk with the small businesses that work out of them every day," Nantel said.
Amazon also warned that the legislation would prohibit its Amazon Flex program as it currently operates, which allows thousands of New Yorkers to earn money through flexible delivery work.
Mamdani's administration has argued that the legislation would improve worker and pedestrian safety.
Amazon countered that it has invested more than $2.5 billion in safety since 2019 and that its serious crash rate in New York City improved by 35.7% from 2024 to 2025. Local delivery drivers have earned nearly $24 an hour on average since January 2025, according to the company.
Cabán has previously accused Amazon of "corporate bullying" over its warnings about higher prices, according to NBC New York .
Amazon said it remains in discussions with City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who has criticized the company's customer outreach campaign while saying lawmakers are working to protect workers without raising prices or costing local jobs.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment, asking whether the administration has conducted an independent economic impact analysis and how the legislation would affect New Yorkers who rely on affordable deliveries of essentials. Fox News Digital did not receive a response as of publication.
Fox News Digital's Eric Mack contributed to this reporting.

articles.title_orig: US Chip Rental Rule Slows China's AI Labs, Beijing Calls In the National Team to Prop Up Stocks
articles.title_zh: US Chip Rental Rule Slows China's AI Labs, Beijing Calls In the National Team to Prop Up Stocks
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.title_zh: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.content_orig:
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.
China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.
Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."
China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.
In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.
His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January
"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.
Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.
Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.
The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ay

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Russian military flotilla bound for Libya turns around after warship sunk on November 22, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Russian military flotilla bound for Libya turns around after warship sunk on November 22, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Italy has denounced Ukraine for carrying out attacks against Russian vessels in Libyan waters, saying it was wrong to “violate Libya’s sovereignty”.
Rome’s rebuke marks a crack in its relationship with Ukraine, which Italy has largely supported since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, including with military assistance.
It coincides with growing concern about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, as well as the risk of other nations being drawn into the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
So why has Italy weighed in now, and what makes Libya so strategically important to Rome?
Kyiv claimed it sank a Russian warship and struck a cargo vessel transporting military equipment off Libya’s coast on Sunday night. The attack on the warship at Benghazi port in eastern Libya killed two naval officers of the self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), according to Libya’s eastern-based forces.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the vessels as legitimate targets, arguing Kyiv had the legal right to defend itself against “Russian aggression”.
He stressed that Ukraine’s actions were “not intended to harm Libya or its people” and that Kyiv respects Libya’s territorial integrity.
“Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere,” Sybiha said in a statement on Telegram.
Musa al-Koni, the vice president of Libya’s Tripoli-based Presidential Council, called the attack “a declaration of war against the Libyan state”.
Libyan authorities “hold the Ukrainian side fully responsible for these terrorist acts”, he added.
The LNA, a rival power that controls eastern and southern parts of Libya and maintains close relations with Russia, promised to retaliate against the Ukrainian attack “at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means”.
Libya is divided between the UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a parallel administration based in Benghazi, backed by the LNA and its renegade commander, Khalifa Haftar.
Italy’s Foreign Minister ⁠⁠Antonio Tajani said it was a mistake for Ukraine to “violate Libya’s sovereignty” and that Rome, which has a small military presence in Libya, had received no prior notice of the operation.
“Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv’s intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port,” Tajani told Italy’s Corriere della Sera newspaper.
Italy’s far-right League party, which is a member of the coalition government, also criticised the attack, saying it risked sowing instability inside Libya.
The comments expose a rare rift with Ukraine, which Italy has largely supported in the war against Russia. Italy has provided Ukraine with more than 3 billion euros ($3.29bn) worth of military aid, according to data from the Kiel Institute think tank, while also backing sweeping sanctions against Russia.
However, there has been division within Italy’s government over further aid to Ukraine, with Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, who heads the League party, opposing more weapons shipments or funding.
Matteo Villa, a senior research fellow at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI), told Al Jazeera that Ukraine’s recent attack off Libya is likely to deepen these domestic tensions.
It “gives Salvini an opportunity to strengthen his case, questioning whether Western military assistance risks enabling Ukraine to pursue objectives that run counter to Italy’s own national interests”, said Villa.
Italy, whose southern islands lie 300km (186 miles) across the Mediterranean from the Libyan coast, has spent years building ties with rival factions in western and eastern Libya.
“Over the past few years, Rome has shifted from almost complete support for the UN-backed Western government in Libya towards building working relationships with the Haftar-controlled East as well,” said Villa.
Italy has also for years helped provide funding, equipment and training for Libya’s maritime authorities, despite reports of migrants being abused and tortured in Libyan custody.
The aim has been to curb irregular migration from Libya to Italy, one of the most perilous and contested Europe-bound routes .
Alessia Melcangi, a nonresident senior fellow with the North Africa Program at the Atlantic Council’s Rafik Hariri Center and Middle East Programs, said Italy’s condemnation of Ukraine partly serves as a form of “damage control” to help Rome balance its competing geopolitical interests.
“Rome needs to demonstrate that its relationships with Kyiv, Tripoli and Benghazi give it meaningful influence over developments affecting its security,” Melcangi told Al Jazeera. “Otherwise, perceptions of exclusion or ambiguity could cause lasting diplomatic damage.”
Villa said Rome’s concerns are fuelled by its geographical proximity to Libya, as well as its economic and strategic interests there, specifically in terms of energy and “migration control”.
“Last year, Libya accounted for roughly a quarter of Italy’s crude oil imports, making it its largest supplier, and the country is by far the main departure point for migrants reaching Italy by sea,” said Villa.
Aldo Liga, a research fellow at the Middle East and North Africa Centre at ISPI, told Al Jazeera that potential escalation that further destabilises Libya would “threaten the security of trade routes and energy flows”, creating a volatile security situation in the Strait of Sicily.
“Instability in Libya is perceived as a direct threat to Italy’s national interests,” he said.
In his interview with Corriere della Sera, Foreign Minister Tajani cited the presence of the Italian military and Italian petroleum company Eni in Libya as being among his concerns about the Ukrainian intervention.
“What happened is worrying,” Tajani said, referring to the Ukrainian attack. “The war between Russia and Ukraine must be prevented from widening, avoiding new outbreaks from occurring.”

articles.title_orig: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
articles.title_zh: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
articles.content_orig:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.
Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.
The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..
"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.
"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."
The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

articles.title_orig: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.title_zh: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.content_orig:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.
Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.
Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".
Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.
All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.
The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.
Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.
One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by  Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".
He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.
"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.
Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.
"So, I believe that young must mobilise."
As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

articles.title_orig: Gold and Silver Jump as Beijing Vows to Support China's Stock Market
articles.title_zh: Gold and Silver Jump as Beijing Vows to Support China's Stock Market
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: S&P cuts France outlook to negative
articles.title_zh: S&P cuts France outlook to negative
articles.content_orig:
Bearish dynamics remain contained in European rates despite the ECB’s tightening bias and firmer energy prices. French spreads tightened ahead of S&P’s review, but political uncertainty and budget risks could warrant a negative outlook – and keep investors cautious
Left on their own with the US out on holiday, European rates briefly tested the upside. While the European Central Bank accounts clearly pointed to the ECB’s tightening bias – maybe even beyond December – and energy prices also sneaked higher as tensions in the Middle East continue to simmer, a bearish dynamic failed to take hold in the end. What lingers is the uncertainty around the tech narrative.
French bond spreads did manage to tighten over the past session, taking the 10y spread over Bunds below the 150bp threshold.
This seems to defy the risk of S&P lowering the outlook on the stable A+ rating it currently still attaches to France. Given the uncertain political backdrop, further budget slippage over the year and an eroding growth outlook, S&P may have enough reason to do just that. At the same time, it would no longer really come as a surprise. Fitch lowered the outlook of its A+ rating to negative at the end of October in an unscheduled move after having only just reviewed the country in August.
Moreover, markets are already pricing France more like a BBB-rated country. To be fair, much of this is likely an overshoot. In its recent Financial Stability Review, the ECB pointed to the procyclical role of hedge funds in eurozone government bond spread dynamics. At the same time, the lingering threat of a downgrade might create another hurdle for investors looking to return to the French bond market.
The Bank of England has reiterated its intention to introduce measures to strengthen the gilt repo market, which could negatively impact demand for gilts. Hedge funds have acted as an important marginal buyer over the past year, helping absorb the significant increase in gilt supply. A popular strategy is buying cash gilts and offsetting these positions with shorts in gilt futures, whereby repo markets offer the ability to leverage up such trades. The slight pricing difference between cash gilts and gilt futures can provide attractive returns. But if the repo costs were to rise, the attractiveness of such trades could fall.
In effect, hedge funds offer balance sheet capacity to house gilts, and therefore any headwinds to such trades can add upward pressure to gilt yields. But the impact is more nuanced. Because the gilt positions are hedged through futures, any unwind of the hedge fund positions should be relatively neutral in terms of term premium. We would, however, expect gilts to underperform swaps. The spread between swaps and gilts is strongly linked to the balance sheet costs of holding bonds. If hedge funds decide a trade is no longer attractive due to higher trading costs, then other players with higher balance sheet costs (such as banks) would have to jump in.
We will see preliminary inflation data for November in France and Spain, where headline rates are expected to ease somewhat but remain at elevated levels. The ECB will also publish its consumer survey on expected inflation. ECB officials scheduled to speak are Chief Economist Philip Lane, Vice President Boris Vujčić, Germany's Joachim Nagel and France's Emmanuel Moulin.
In primary markets, Italy will auction 5y and 10y BTPS as well as 8y and 9y CCTeu floaters (in total up to 8bn).

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Nvidia chips on sale for $3M in China — as Jensen Huang scandal and US crackdown chokes supply
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Nvidia chips on sale for $3M in China — as Jensen Huang scandal and US crackdown chokes supply
articles.content_orig:
Chinese videos are advertising banned Nvidia chips for sale at $3 million apiece , more than five times the US price.
Prices have spiked amid a crackdown by both Washington and the chip maker on the processors after investigations found they had been making their way into the market.
In one Shenzhen video on Douyin , China’s version of TikTok, a young woman from the “Compute Sisters” account shows off a machine billed as an Nvidia B300 server.
The server costs about $550,000 in the US and packs eight of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips , enough to run reasoning models such as China’s DeepSeek-R1.
“The market for Nvidia high-end chips is crazy right now,” a trader who deals in high-performance chips told The Post, requesting anonymity. “My friends who were in this business made about [$15 million] per month, just by selling B300 and other AI chips.”
The trader gives the boom “another two or three months” before everything’s cut off.
“Whatever Nvidia has already shipped, or is on the way, that’s all there is,” the trader said. “After that, it will probably be very hard to get any more into China.”
In the wake of revelations about CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (who is not related to him), Washington tightened the rules on Chinese firms buying and renting computing power overseas.
Nvidia has also told its manufacturing partners to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.
He expects the price of this eight-chip server to climb to as much as $4.5 million, within two months. One Douyin account put the current price at 23 million yuan ($3.4 million) and claimed it still had buyers lined up.
However, The Post couldn’t verify the online pitches, and many could be scams.
“Anyone posting on WeChat that they have stock is just a middleman,” one source in tech hub Shenzhen told The Post.
Vendors at Shenzhen’s sprawling Huaqiangbei electronics market were asking as much as $3.4 million for a single eight-chip Nvidia B300 server, The Washington Post reported this week, asking for a deposit before they’d even show chips to a reporter.
In Taiwan, prosecutors allege one group shipped 74 B300 servers to customers in China, clearing roughly $21 million.
Following revelations about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang , Washington blacklisted Megaspeed , the company she worked for. Jensen resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, but Nvidia’s board reinstated him 11 days later .
US intelligence officials told Congress Alice had been in contact with a Chinese intelligence officer, but they had no indication she’d been asked to spy on Jensen , CBS News reported. Beijing denies she is a spy and she has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
On Friday, Bloomberg reported two Chinese firms had installed Nvidia’s restricted Blackwell chips at a Shanghai data center, which had been linked to Alice Huang.
Jensen is due to answer lawmakers’ questions privately on Dec. 1.
US companies also figure in the overseas chip trade. CBS News found that two California companies controlled by Chinese-owned firms bought advanced Nvidia chips and some of that hardware was later leased or sold to firms in Southeast Asia. US authorities have not accused either California company of wrongdoing.
Asia buys tens of billions of dollars’ worth of AI chips a year, and Washington has “zero visibility into these sales,” according to Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council official who helped write the export rules.
For years, Chinese AI labs could train models on Nvidia chips by renting time at data centers in other Southeast Asian countries. Those chips never had to enter China and violate any export restrictions. Under a US rule that took effect Nov. 19 , those data centers now need US approval to give Chinese labs access to large clusters of advanced chips.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.
Anyone hoping to get an advanced chip in China faces a minefield.
The prospect of a payday has drawn gold dealers, former bitcoin miners and even beauty salon owners into the trade, Chinese business magazine Caijing reported.
One broker said he flew from Nanjing to Shenzhen and followed a tip someone had Nvidia B300s to sell. He counted 40 or 50 people in the lobby, waiting. Everyone he asked was another middleman, the magazine said.
“There are too many traps in this circle,” the Shenzhen source told The Post.

articles.title_orig: Kyiv offers Black Sea ceasefire to protect grain exports
articles.title_zh: Kyiv offers Black Sea ceasefire to protect grain exports
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.
“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.
Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.
He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.
The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters , and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.
A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.
In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.
International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.
On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.
The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.
In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.
“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.
He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.
“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.
After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.
Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Economist labels Trump ‘the biggest loser of any president’ as he shreds key trade policy
articles.title_zh: Economist labels Trump ‘the biggest loser of any president’ as he shreds key trade policy
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Financial commentator and stockbroker Peter Schiff took aim at Donald Trump 's trade policies Friday, calling him "the biggest loser of any president" as the U.S. goods trade deficit continues to widen despite the president’s aggressive tariffs .
Schiff's comments came after the goods trade deficit jumped 10.7 percent to $149.5 billion in October, according to the Census Bureau's latest advance report . For this year, imports totaled $365.3 billion, while exports came in at just $215.8 billion.
The gap was more than double what it was in October 2025.
“It was the third-largest monthly deficit in history, exceeded only by January and March of 2025, when importers rushed to avoid tariffs,” Schiff said. “On trade, Trump is the biggest loser of any president,” he wrote on X .
The deficit has also climbed steadily in recent months, rising from $118.9 billion in July.
The latest numbers come as Trump continues to defend his tariffs , which have been a major part of his economic agenda during his second term.
Trump previously pointed to a 55 percent drop in the trade deficit in April 2026 as a sign that his tariffs were working. He celebrated the numbers on Truth Social , writing , “THANK YOU MR. TARIFF !”
But the deficit has since climbed again, putting Trump's claims about the success of his trade policies under fresh scrutiny.
Trump has continued pushing new tariffs despite mounting political and legal challenges. On Wednesday, his administration announced proposed import taxes on goods from China, the European Union and 12 other trading partners.
The administration says the tariffs are meant to stop foreign countries from making too many goods and selling them cheaply, arguing that government subsidies and other trade practices give overseas companies an unfair advantage over U.S. manufacturers.
China could face tariffs of up to 20 percent , while the proposed rates for other trading partners range from 15 percent to 35 percent, depending on the country. The measures are not final, and the administration is accepting public comments before taking further action.
The latest proposals also come after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping 2025 tariffs earlier this year, forcing the administration to pursue a different legal path to impose import taxes.
Schiff, who serves as chief economist and global strategist at Euro Pacific Asset Management and hosts “The Peter Schiff Show,” an investing podcast, is no stranger to criticizing Trump's economic policies.
The stockbroker also clashed with Trump last year after appearing on Fox News. Trump later called Schiff a “Trump-hating loser who has already proven to be wrong.”

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: U.S. forces disable commercial ship that allegedly tried to breach blockade on Iranian ports
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: U.S. forces disable commercial ship that allegedly tried to breach blockade on Iranian ports
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military has disabled a merchant ship in the Gulf of Oman that was trying to run its blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said Friday.
A military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," it said in a statement.
According to U.S. Central Command, the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel's destination as Singapore.
The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations "that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region's waters."
The strike comes as the Trump administration weighs its options in the long-simmering war with Iran, which began at the end of February and has settled into a quiet stalemate in the past several months.
Earlier in November, officials in the region told The Associated Press that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the U.S. to restart the war or allow Israel to launch airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities and missile capabilities.
Meanwhile, government and security officials from the Persian Gulf countries, as well as Pakistan and Turkey, were engaged in a diplomatic campaign, which included phone calls with senior U.S. officials, to stave off a renewed war in the region.
President Donald Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the war "militarily is effectively over."
The U.S. military has maintained a sizable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.
The U.S. has been blockading Iranian ports since April, though the blockade was lifted in the summer during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the U.S. military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabling those that refuse to comply.
The Pacific Archer is at least the 15th disclosed vessel to be disabled by the U.S. military since the blockade began in the spring and the sixth since it resumed this summer. The previous vessel was disabled on Nov. 7.
In June, the practice drew condemnation when a military strike on a Guinea-Bissau-flagged tanker attempting to evade the American blockade resulted in three deaths.
Three Indian sailors were killed when American forces struck the Palau-flagged M/T Settebello, officials in India said at the time. The leader of the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency, condemned the attack.
U.S. Central Command has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.
The claims could not be independently verified.
In a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster, the country's Revolutionary Guard also said the number of oil tankers attempting to transit through unauthorized routes in the critical waterway has sharply decreased in recent days.
Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without approval from Tehran.
Oil flows in the first two weeks of November fell by around 20% to around 13 million barrels per day compared with October, when exports roughly equaled the prewar amounts of 15-16 million barrels per day, according to Rystad Energy.
Reasons for the November decline include Iranian attacks that discourage tankers from attempting the strait crossing and reduced flows through a key Saudi pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has also been attacked several times.
A report by U.N. Trade and Development finds that disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal are lengthening voyages, raising fuel costs, driving port congestion and adding to uncertainty. Alternative ports, inland transport and logistics arrangements have kept trade moving, but at a higher cost.
Toqa Ezzidin in Cairo contributed.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.content_orig:
Hackers penetrated the Air Force’s cloud computing platform in a breach that could have exposed sensitive military information, a U.S. official said Friday.
The official confirmed the hack to NBC News but could not  provide any additional information about timing or the attack’s impact.
“The department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems,” an Air Force spokesperson said.
Reuters first reported about this most recent cyberintrusion against federal assets.
The FBI’s National Crime Information Center — which is used by federal, state and local authorities to share important information — was recently breached, sources briefed on the matter told NBC News this week .
And about two months ago, the FBI and Dutch national police arrested leaders of a “global cybercrime and threat actor group” that allegedly stole employee information from a bureau database. It is unclear whether any of these breaches are related.
“We continuously take prudent measures to protect department information, systems, and mission capabilities,” the Air Force spokesperson said Friday. “Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority.”
“The department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet, evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements,” the statement continued. “Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk management processes.”
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Gordon Lubold is a national security reporter for NBC News.
